interactions.summary: Students ask whether Jiang's account of will resembles Nietzsche or psychology's self-efficacy, and Jiang says yes, renaming the whole logic as manifestation and linking it to Nietzsche's will to power.

A student asks whether Piccarda simply failed to want escape or ascent strongly enough, and Jiang deepens the scenario by reconstructing her fear inside the convent under threat from violent soldiers.
interactions.speaker_attribution: student clarification with Jiang guided thought experiment

speaker_notes.note: Jiang's claim that there is 'really no good and evil in the universe, there's just will' is a provocative classroom compression attached to this interpretive frame, not a settled repository-wide metaphysical canon statement.

claims.claim: A student explicitly asks whether Jiang's Dantean model of will is the same as Nietzsche's will to power.
Another student links the same model to self-efficacy: belief in one's own ability is the main condition for accomplishing a goal.
Jiang answers that the popular term for this mechanism is manifestation: you imagine something because you will it into being, which he says is also Nietzsche's point.
Jiang radically compresses the metaphysics by saying that beneath moral categories there is really only will, and one's life becomes a matter of how that will is lived out.
A student asks for clarification by restating the practical consequence: perhaps Piccarda neither wanted escape enough nor wanted ascent strongly enough.
Jiang responds by reconstructing Piccarda's inner scene under coercion: fear of violent soldiers and concern for everyone in the convent become the emotional test of what her will is actually doing.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang fuses Dante, Nietzsche, and pop self-help into one sentence: manifestation is willing an imagined future into being.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you imagine it but you're able to imagine because you will it into being
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest conceptual compression and shows how Jiang modernizes the free-will framework for the classroom.

signature_moments.moment: Moral language gets displaced by a more primal axis: not good and evil, but the force and direction of will.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's really no good and evil in the universe there's just will
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most provocative sentence and raises the stakes for how later fear and trust will be interpreted.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang forces the metaphysics back into lived experience by asking the class to inhabit Piccarda's fear with soldiers at the gate.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's like an army outside the convent demanding that she go with them
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It prevents the will discussion from staying abstract and sets up fear itself as the next diagnostic object.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A student's psychology comparison for Jiang's will-model: accomplishment depends first on believing that one can do the thing.
The Nietzschean comparison the class uses to understand Jiang's claim that will imagines and manifests its own path.

chronology_notes.note: After defining will through manifestation, the lecture broadens the comparison set to Nietzsche and psychology, then immediately returns to Piccarda's emotional state under coercion. The abstract model is being tested against fear, trust, and concrete danger.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's 'no good and evil, just will' line is rhetorically compressed and may overstate for effect. Preserve it as a charged classroom formulation rather than a cleaned-up doctrinal thesis.
